look_here_first: JOHNSONGRASS (INTRODUCED, INVASIVE): rather tall PERENNIAL Sorghum with broad flat leaves sometimes showing pale white midrib and often an OPEN purplish panicle. Neither color nor a white midrib proves ID. STRONG CONFIRMATION is long, creeping, jointed SCALY UNDERGROUND RHIZOMES with root-bearing nodes, seen in the existing actual Austin source photo. A true collar photo shows a fringe of hairs at the membranous ligule region (membrane length not measured). Fertile sessile spikelet plus companion pedicelled unit needs an intact mature macro. Don't dig or transport viable rhizome fragments unnecessarily.

best_field_traits: Robust warm-season perennial grass, usually 0.5–2 m tall but sometimes taller; heavy loose stands in roadside ditches, drainage bottoms and disturbed restoration soils.
Broad flat grass leaf blades (FNA ~8–40 mm wide, ~10–90 cm long), generally with conspicuous pale central midrib; do not trust white midrib alone.
Ligule 2–6 mm, MEMBRANOUS and conspicuously ciliate (fringed with hairs), NOT merely a solid membrane or pure hair tuft. No auricles.
Large terminal, branched, somewhat triangular/pyramidal open panicle often 10–50 cm long, green to reddish/purple then tan; may partially contract late.
Short terminal racelets on branches with paired sorghum spikelets: one sessile bisexual/fertile, one pedicelled usually staminate; callus and glumes require macro.
Strong creeping underground rhizomes, whitish/tan and scaly, many jointed nodes and buds; may repeatedly resprout from fragments.
Don't confuse native Sorghastrum nutans: highly reduced/vestigial pedicellate companion instead of a full Sorghum spikelet; two look similar in a tall grass stand.
morphology_keys.habit: Perennial C4 warm-season coarse grass, usually robust upright culms from an underground branching rhizome system; colonies expand from both seed and vegetative buds.
morphology_keys.culm: Flowering stalks commonly 50–200 cm tall (FNA; taller exceptional stands exist), obvious grass nodes; leaf sheaths enclose culm; nodes sometimes appressed-hairy.
morphology_keys.leaf_blade: Flat, coarse, long linear leaves with pale/light central midvein, typically 8–40 mm broad. Width, color and midrib vary; blade margins often rough.
morphology_keys.sheath: Leaf sheath around culm, generally smooth, true grass blade-sheath collar present. Trace same culm from leaf to collar to node when identifying.
morphology_keys.ligule: At inner junction of sheath and blade, conspicuously ciliate 2–6 mm thin translucent membrane. Avoid vague 'hairy ligule' descriptions that hide membrane.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: Large loose open 10–50(-55) cm branched terminal panicle, 5–25 cm wide (FNA/GrassBase); primary branches divided into short paired-spikelet-bearing raceme units. May be purplish at flowering, straw colored at maturity.
morphology_keys.spikelet_pair: A sessile larger typically bisexual fertile spikelet (no little stalk) and a complete pedicelled staminate companion spikelet (on slender short stalk); confirm under magnification on a short panicle branch.
morphology_keys.sessile_spikelet: FNA 3.8–6.5 mm long and 1.5–2.3 mm wide, hard/shiny glumes, awn absent or bent/twisted to ~13 mm. Do not identify a detached immature organ as sessile without base attachment.
morphology_keys.pedicelled_spikelet: FNA ~3.6–5.6 mm; usually staminate; mounted on small pedicel ~1.8–3.3 mm. Full companion unlike highly reduced vestige of Sorghastrum.
morphology_keys.fruit: Grass caryopsis enclosed by the spikelet; mature head often shatters naturally below the sessile spikelet. Do not deliberately shake invasive seeded heads to demonstrate dispersal.
morphology_keys.rhizome: Firm creeping BELOWGROUND stem with scaly sheath remnants at nodes, buds and connected shoots; many occur in top ~20 cm soil, deeper possible. Distinguish true nodes and shoots from fibrous ROOTS.
morphology_keys.roots: Fine fibrous roots from stem bases and rhizome nodes; lateral root ≠ rhizome unless buds and stem joints are present.
morphology_keys.season: Warm-season growth and flowering/seed production; returns from rhizomes after frost and mowing when viable.
morphology_keys.habitat: Roadside grass edges, disturbed sunny prairie and restoration beds, drainages, wet ditches and stream banks, cultivated fields, disturbed grassland patches. Introduced throughout Texas.
morphology_keys.caution: Perennial rhizomes and open panicle distinguish it from many natives/annuals only as combined characters; shattercane and sorghum hybrids can overlap.

One intact mature sessile fertile and pedicelled spikelet pair, mm scale
Whole plant including inflorescence, leaf white midrib and base from same ID-vouchered specimen

crew_key: 1 · Broad blade with obvious white midrib: possible Johnsongrass, NOT ID proof.
2 · Pull back blade gently to inspect a 2–6 mm CILIATE MEMBRANOUS ligule; no auricles.
3 · Full mature head: large open branchy panicle, not single turkeyfoot, uniform foxtail cylinder or pure V-shaped arms.

4 · Lift a small disturbed-edge sample of BELOWGROUND runners: cream scaly horizontal STEMS with nodes/buds and connected shoots → strongly favors Johnsongrass; fibrous roots without nodes are different.
5 · Macro paired spikelets at panicle branchlet tips: directly attached sessile fertile + a stalked pedicelled companion.
6 · If native Indiangrass/switchgrass or shattercane remains plausible, mark Sorghum sp./grass ID uncertain; do not label grass invasive from midrib alone.
comparisons.warning: Especially in native restored prairie, protect Indiangrass, switchgrass, and big bluestem from false Johnson grass IDs. Panicle color and single white midrib are not sufficient. Some feral bicolor hybrids obscure standard distinctions.

taxonomic_note: Sorghum halepense (L.) Pers., accepted Kew Poaceae species, native to parts of Eurasia, northern Africa and Indo-China, introduced in Texas. Shattercane is generally weedy Sorghum bicolor, and hybrid 'S. almum' or bicolor × halepense complexes can blur diagnostic traits. The actual native Sorghastrum nutans (Indiangrass) shares large grass form but not Sorghum's complete spikelet pairs. Never treat all open panicles or white midribs as Johnsongrass.

family_genus_teaching.family: Poaceae: culm node, leaf sheath, ligule, blade, inflorescence, spikelet containing lemma and palea; separate branches from individual spikelets.
family_genus_teaching.genus: Sorghum panicles terminate in short units of PAIRS: sessile fertile spikelet and developed pedicelled companion. Do not mistake a branching panicle silhouette for genus proof.
family_genus_teaching.species: Sorghum halepense is tall, perennial, spreading via scaly underground rhizomes; has 2–6 mm ciliate membranous ligule and open panicle. Texas INTRODUCED.
family_genus_teaching.crew_question: Can you show the white midrib, the actual hairy-EDGED LIGULE MEMBRANE, intact RHIZOME with buds/nodes and one SESSILE+PEDICELLED spikelet pair in separate photos?

ecological_notes.origin_status: Introduced to Texas; Eurasian/Macaronesian/African historical range (Kew accepted introduced Texas); keep native score excluded.
ecological_notes.impact: Dense persistent rhizomatous colonies displace diverse native forb/grass recruitment on disturbed sunny sites and native restoration margins. Seed and rhizome fragments both spread the infestation.
ecological_notes.soil_role: Can provide cover and forage and temporary erosion reduction; those uses do not make it a locally native ecosystem-restoration plant.
ecological_notes.management: Mark rhizome-linked patch edge and seed source. For manual removal, recover intact rhizomes and repeated re-sprouts; don't cultivate or move fresh rhizomes into clean native areas. Expect multi-season follow-up. Prevent seed distribution along equipment routes.
ecological_notes.livestock_safety: Sorghum halepense can accumulate cyanogenic potential (prussic acid risk), especially stressed/frosted/young regrowth; nitrate risk may also arise under some conditions. Do not feed unknown stressed Sorghum cuttings to grazing animals; consult local extension guidance.
ecological_notes.nonchemical: On small restoration patches, careful repeated digging of rhizomes plus repeat patrol is preferable to one-off clipping; long-term suppression may require coordinated multi-year management of both belowground reserves and seed rain.
ecological_notes.photo_handling: For educational specimens, photograph rhizomes exposed by necessary work rather than fragmenting intact prairie soil or dispersing ripe invasive seed.
ecological_notes.lep_bee_note: No fabricated host insect counts or native ecological score; only exact confirmed host links should appear.

visual_comparison.title: JOHNSONGRASS — see true panicle, midrib, rhizome and ligule
visual_comparison.subtitle: Johnsongrass's own actual habit, ligule-region, rhizome and flowering gallery, followed by three clearly distinct native Indiangrass and introduced Sorghum bicolor comparative photographs. Matching anatomy is not interchangeable; verify distinctive floral pairing, leaf midrib, and rhizomes.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: JOHNSONGRASS (EXOTIC): often prominent WHITE MIDRIB + broad leaves, open panicle, developed paired sessile/pedicelled spikelets, long jointed creeping rhizomes. INDIANGRASS (NATIVE): prominent rifle-sight collar, bent-awn fertile spikelet and naked reduced companion pedicel. GRAIN SORGHUM (EXOTIC crop): often annual without creeping rhizomes. Do not identify or remove from one trait alone.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Johnsongrass — underground RHIZOME first, then collar and paired spikelets
steps: START BELOWGROUND: follow the pale horizontal jointed underground stem and its attached fine roots in the real Austin rhizome photograph. Johnsongrass regrows from these scaly rhizomes; don't confuse them with fibrous roots.
LOOK AT THE COLLAR: the Matt Lavin closeup shows dense pale fringe near the blade/sheath join. Only measure true membranous ligule length after gently exposing it with a 1-mm rule.
FOLLOW THE FLOWERING HEAD: an open often reddish branching panicle supports Johnsongrass, but crop sorghum and shattercane can overlap in head appearance.
VIEW THE STIGMA: the original Linda Jo Conn arrow points at feathery stigma, NOT at a sessile/pedicelled pair. Observe an entire attached mature branchlet to distinguish two spikelet partners.

COMPARE MATURE SORGHUM PAIR at 10–20x: sessile fertile and adjacent pedicelled sterile/staminate spikelet must both be visible, along with actual glumes, pedicel and axis internode, before applying measured arrows.

CHECK THE ROOTSTOCK AGAINST S. BICOLOR: annual cultivated/escaped sorghum generally lacks the creeping scaly rhizome network. Midrib whiteness, head color and height never establish the split by themselves.
CONTROL SPREAD: document or collect underground tissue only when legally permitted; remove all viable pieces from equipment and prevent fragment transport.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: The physically photographed creeping segmented rhizome is the strongest Johnsongrass-versus-grain-sorghum cue; complete attached spikelet pairs and true ligule measurements remain absent.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Ten existing exact-species local photo records, but only five were in the canonical visual gallery before this lane-2 pass. Three more real source images connected without inventing pixel arrows. Rhizome bud locations, ligule membrane length, paired spikelet measurements and live Pages QA remain unverified.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — RHIZOMES PLUS OPEN PANICLE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Tall warm-season perennial with a 10–50 cm open branched head and creeping scaly underground stems.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Look for broad leaves with a pale midrib, but never identify Johnsongrass from a white midrib or purple panicle alone. A real archived Austin-area photograph shows a jointed underground rhizome; trace nodes and connected shoots to distinguish a STEM from a fibrous root. Do not dig, move, or scatter viable invasive rhizome fragments merely to confirm an ID.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL RHIZOME PHOTO — SCALE AND AXILLARY BUD DETAIL MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE TRUE LEAF COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.short: True ligule is a 2–6 mm membranous flap with a conspicuous ciliate fringe; auricles absent.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Peel back the blade at the sheath junction and separate the translucent membrane from its fringe of hairs. The archived Matt Lavin source photo resolves collar hairs, NOT a measurable 2–6 mm membrane edge. Do not draw an arrow to a membrane hidden by the photographed angle; capture a second opened view with a 1-mm ruler.
field_id_short_tiles.status: COLLAR FRINGE VISIBLE — TRUE MEMBRANE MEASUREMENT MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · TWO DIFFERENT SPIKELETS FORM A PAIR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Sessile fertile spikelet 3.8–6.5 mm; pedicelled companion 3.6–5.6 mm on a 1.8–3.3 mm stalk.
field_id_short_tiles.details: At 10–20× trace a short panicle branch to a spikelet without a stalk and its complete stalked companion. The sessile unit usually has bisexual reproductive organs; the pedicelled unit is usually staminate. The sessile spikelet is enclosed by two hardened shiny glumes, while the pedicelled glumes may be thinner. Preserve each attachment in a single photograph with a 1-mm ruler; no existing macro independently establishes the full pair.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FNA MEASUREMENTS — ATTACHED PAIRED-SPIKELET MACRO MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · SEPARATE GLUMES, LEMMAS AND OPTIONAL AWN
field_id_short_tiles.short: Sessile glumes enclose the florets; lower sterile lemma about 3.5–5 mm, fertile lemma about 2–4 mm; awn variable.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Dissect one mature sessile spikelet. Do not confuse the firm shiny OUTER glumes with the thinner INNER lemmas. Kew GrassBase describes a 3.5–5 mm lower sterile lemma and 2–4 mm fertile lemma, sometimes bearing one bent/twisted awn; FNA reports awns absent or up to about 13 mm, while other treatments extend the range. No photograph currently supports a precise awn-origin arrow or species determination from awn length alone.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PUBLISHED ANATOMY — DISSECTED MEASURED LEMMAS MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · PROTECT NATIVE GRASS LOOK-ALIKES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Native Indiangrass has a strongly reduced pedicelled companion; switchgrass has different small panicle spikelets.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Sorghastrum nutans has a highly reduced or vestigial pedicelled unit, unlike the developed companion of Sorghum; Panicum virgatum lacks the characteristic sorghum pair. Crop/feral S. bicolor generally lacks extensive creeping scaly rhizomes, but shattercane and hybrids can overlap. Confirm intact spikelets and underground growth before removing a native-looking tall grass; record Sorghum sp. when uncertain.
field_id_short_tiles.status: CREW LOOK-ALIKE KEY — MATCHED RIPE MACROS MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE AND EXACT HANDOFF
field_id_short_tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — useful rhizome and collar photos exist; paired-spikelet anatomy is still unproven.
field_id_short_tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: same-plant rhizome node and axillary bud with 1-cm scale; opened 2–6 mm ciliate membrane with 1-mm scale; mature attached sessile/pedicelled pair with glumes and detached sterile/fertile lemmas plus actual awn insertion at 10–40×; same-scale Indiangrass, switchgrass and grain-sorghum comparisons.
